claim: Induction of a DSB in human cells causes local nucleosome disassembly, apparently independently from DNA end resection.
source: Here we show that induction of a DSB in human cells causes local nucleosome disassembly, apparently independently from DNA end resection.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing nucleosome disassembly around DSBs without significant DNA resection.

claim: The efficient removal of histone H3 from the genome during non-homologous end joining was promoted by both ATM and the ATP-dependent nucleosome remodeler INO80.
source: This efficient removal of histone H3 from the genome during non-homologous end joining was promoted by both ATM and the ATP-dependent nucleosome remodeler INO80.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ATM inhibition and INO80 knockdown experiments showing their roles in histone H3 removal.

claim: Chromatin reassembly during DSB repair was dependent on the HIRA histone chaperone that is specific to the replication-independent histone variant H3.3.
source: Chromatin reassembly during DSB repair was dependent on the HIRA histone chaperone that is specific to the replication-independent histone variant H3.3 and on CAF-1 that is specific to the replication-dependent canonical histones H3.1/H3.2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from HIRA knockdown experiments showing defects in chromatin reassembly.

claim: Chromatin reassembly during DSB repair was dependent on CAF-1 that is specific to the replication-dependent canonical histones H3.1/H3.2.
source: Chromatin reassembly during DSB repair was dependent on the HIRA histone chaperone that is specific to the replication-independent histone variant H3.3 and on CAF-1 that is specific to the replication-dependent canonical histones H3.1/H3.2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from CAF-1 knockdown experiments showing defects in chromatin reassembly.

claim: The epigenetic information is re-established after DSB repair by the concerted and interdependent action of replication-independent and replication-dependent chromatin assembly pathways.
source: Our data suggest that the epigenetic information is re-established after DSB repair by the concerted and interdependent action of replication-independent and replication-dependent chromatin assembly pathways.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing both HIRA and CAF-1 are required for chromatin reassembly.

claim: DNA double-strand breaks occur intrinsically during normal cell metabolism, or are caused by exogenous agents, such as ionizing radiation or some classes of chemotherapeutic drugs.
source: DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) occur intrinsically during normal cell metabolism, or are caused by exogenous agents, such as ionizing radiation (IR) or some classes of chemotherapeutic drugs.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about DNA damage sources.

claim: DSBs are essential intermediates during programmed recombination events, such as meiosis, budding yeast mating-type switching, and lymphocyte development.
source: In addition, DSBs are essential intermediates during programmed recombination events, such as meiosis, budding yeast mating-type switching, and lymphocyte development (Mimitou and Symington, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Eukaryotic cells have evolved two mechanistically distinct pathways to repair DSBs: non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) and homologous recombination (HR).
source: Eukaryotic cells have evolved two mechanistically distinct pathways to repair DSBs: non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) and homologous recombination (HR) (Ceccaldi et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and represents established knowledge.

claim: In mammalian cells NHEJ is responsible for repairing the majority of DSBs throughout the cell cycle.
source: In mammalian cells NHEJ is responsible for repairing the majority of DSBs throughout the cell cycle, while HR is mostly active in late S and G2 phases when a sister homolog is present (Kass and Jasin, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: HR is mostly active in late S and G2 phases when a sister homolog is present.
source: In mammalian cells NHEJ is responsible for repairing the majority of DSBs throughout the cell cycle, while HR is mostly active in late S and G2 phases when a sister homolog is present (Kass and Jasin, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The nucleosome is the primary level of chromatin structure, with about 146 bp of DNA wrapped around an octamer of histones, which includes two molecules each of histones H2A, H2B, H3 and H4.
source: The nucleosome is the primary level of chromatin structure, with about 146 bp of DNA wrapped around an octamer of histones, which includes two molecules each of histones H2A, H2B, H3 and H4 (van Holde, 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and represents established knowledge about nucleosome structure.

claim: Complete nucleosome disassembly, indicated by the removal of histone H3 from the DNA, has been observed in the vicinity of an unrepairable DSB undergoing extensive resection in budding yeast.
source: Complete nucleosome disassembly, indicated by the removal of histone H3 from the DNA, has been observed in the vicinity of an unrepairable DSB undergoing extensive resection in budding yeast (Tsukuda et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work in yeast.

claim: Chromatin disassembly in budding yeast was dependent on MRE11 and the INO80 ATP-dependent nucleosome remodeling complex.
source: This chromatin disassembly was dependent on MRE11 and the INO80 ATP-dependent nucleosome remodeling complex (Tsukuda et al., 2005), both of which are required, either directly or indirectly, for timely DNA resection (Paull and Gellert, 1998; van Attikum et al., 2004; Gospodinov et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work in yeast.

claim: MRE11 and INO80 are required, either directly or indirectly, for timely DNA resection.
source: This chromatin disassembly was dependent on MRE11 and the INO80 ATP-dependent nucleosome remodeling complex (Tsukuda et al., 2005), both of which are required, either directly or indirectly, for timely DNA resection (Paull and Gellert, 1998; van Attikum et al., 2004; Gospodinov et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: During HR in yeast, at least some nucleosomes are disassembled from around DSBs.
source: Similarly, during HR in yeast, at least some nucleosomes are disassembled from around DSBs, because inhibition of the chromatin reassembly process reduced the local histone occupancy after DSB repair (Chen et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and inference from chromatin reassembly experiments.

claim: Displacement of histones H2B and H3 was apparent during DSB repair around DSBs that were generated by introduction of the I-PpoI and HO homing enzymes into mammalian cells.
source: Displacement of histones H2B and H3 was apparent during DSB repair around DSBs that were generated by introduction of the I-PpoI and HO homing enzymes into mammalian cells (Goldstein et al., 2013; Sunavala-Dossabhoy and De Benedetti, 2009; Berkovich et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work in mammalian cells.

claim: The displacement of H2B from the periphery of nucleosomes around a DSB in mammalian cells was dependent on NBS1, a component of the MRE11-RAD50-NBS1 DNA end resection complex.
source: Using these systems, the displacement of H2B from the periphery of nucleosomes around a DSB in mammalian cells was dependent on NBS1, a component of the MRE11-RAD50-NBS1 DNA end resection complex (Berkovich et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Loss of H3 was only observed in cycling cells, not in cells arrested in G1 phase.
source: In agreement with the idea that DNA end resection drives nucleosome disassembly, loss of H3, which resides in the central part of the nucleosome and is indicative of disassembly of the entire nucleosome, was only observed in cycling cells (Goldstein et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In cells arrested in G1 phase, which can only repair DSBs by NHEJ, only H2A-H2B were removed during DSB repair not H3-H4.
source: In cells arrested in G1 phase, which can only repair DSBs by NHEJ, only H2A-H2B were removed during DSB repair not H3-H4.
evidence: This claim is based on prior work cited in the manuscript.

claim: Only partial, not complete nucleosome disassembly, accompanies NHEJ in mammalian cells according to prior work.
source: This suggested that only partial, not complete nucleosome disassembly, accompanies NHEJ in mammalian cells.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from prior work cited in the manuscript.

claim: In yeast, the H3-H4 histone chaperone Asf1 is required for chromatin assembly after HR repair.
source: In yeast, the H3-H4 histone chaperone Asf1 is required for chromatin assembly after HR repair, but this function is due to the role of Asf1 in promoting acetylation of histone H3 on lysine 56 (Chen et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The function of Asf1 in chromatin assembly after HR repair in yeast is due to the role of Asf1 in promoting acetylation of histone H3 on lysine 56.
source: In yeast, the H3-H4 histone chaperone Asf1 is required for chromatin assembly after HR repair, but this function is due to the role of Asf1 in promoting acetylation of histone H3 on lysine 56 (Chen et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Nucleolin was shown to be involved in nucleosome disruption in the vicinity of a DSB within the rDNA locus in human cells.
source: Nucleolin, a nucloeolar histone chaperone for H2A-H2B, was shown to be involved in nucleosome disruption in the vicinity of a DSB within the rDNA locus in human cells (Goldstein et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The histone chaperone CAF-1 deposits newly-synthesized H3/H4 onto the DNA following DNA replication and nucleotide excision repair in vitro and in cells.
source: The histone chaperone CAF-1 deposits newly-synthesized H3/H4 onto the DNA following DNA replication and nucleotide excision repair (NER) in vitro and in cells (Gaillard et al., 1996; Smith and Stillman, 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: HIRA deposits the histone variant H3.3/H4 onto the genome at times other than DNA synthesis, particularly during transcription.
source: Another histone chaperone, HIRA, deposits the histone variant H3.3/H4 onto the genome at times other than DNA synthesis, particularly during transcription (Ray-Gallet et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Mammalian ASF1A predominantly delivers the H3.3/H4 to HIRA for replication-independent chromatin assembly.
source: The histone chaperone ASF1 donates the histones to CAF-1 and HIRA, where mammalian ASF1A predominantly delivers the H3.3/H4 to HIRA for replication-independent chromatin assembly and ASF1B predominantly delivers H3.1/H4 to CAF-1 for replication-dependent chromatin assembly (Tagami et al., 2004; Tyler et al., 2001; Gurard-Levin et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: ASF1B predominantly delivers H3.1/H4 to CAF-1 for replication-dependent chromatin assembly.
source: The histone chaperone ASF1 donates the histones to CAF-1 and HIRA, where mammalian ASF1A predominantly delivers the H3.3/H4 to HIRA for replication-independent chromatin assembly and ASF1B predominantly delivers H3.1/H4 to CAF-1 for replication-dependent chromatin assembly (Tagami et al., 2004; Tyler et al., 2001; Gurard-Levin et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: During NER and prior to the assembly of H3.1 into chromatin, HIRA assembles H3.3 into the chromatin around UV lesions.
source: During NER and prior to the assembly of H3.1 into chromatin, HIRA assembles H3.3 into the chromatin around UV lesions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Transient deposition of H3.3 primes the chromatin for later recovery of transcription after repair of UV lesions by NER.
source: This transient deposition of H3.3 primes the chromatin for later recovery of transcription after repair of UV lesions by NER (Adam et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: At 3 hr after addition of tamoxifen to HEK-293 cells, the I-PpoI site within the SLCO5A1 gene was about 50% cleaved in the cell population.
source: At 3 hr after addition of tamoxifen to HEK-293 cells to stimulate nuclear localization, the I-PpoI site within the SLCO5A1 gene was about 50% cleaved in the cell population, as determined by PCR over the I-PpoI site using flanking primers (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The DNA level at the I-PpoI site was restored back to over 95% at 6–8 hr, indicating that most of the DSBs had been repaired.
source: The DNA level at the I-PpoI site was restored back to over 95% at 6–8 hr, indicating that most of the DSBs had been repaired.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Complete local nucleosome disassembly and reassembly occurred during DSB repair, as indicated by ChIP analysis of H3 around the I-PpoI break sites within the SLCO5A1 gene.
source: Complete local nucleosome disassembly and reassembly occurred during DSB repair, as indicated by ChIP analysis of H3 around the I-PpoI break sites within the SLCO5A1 gene (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Nucleosomes adjacent to the break were disassembled completely from around all the DSBs in the population, because histone occupancy dropped to 50% at the three-hour time point at which 50% of the DNA was cleaved.
source: Furthermore, it appears that nucleosomes adjacent to the break were disassembled completely from around all the DSBs in the population, because histone occupancy dropped to 50% at the three-hour time point at which 50% of the DNA was cleaved.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing correlation between DNA cutting and histone loss.

claim: Histone occupancy returned to the pre-damage levels at the 6–8 hr time point, which is the same time point at which the DNA lesion is approximately 100% repaired.
source: Histone occupancy returned to the pre-damage levels at the 6–8 hr time point, which is the same time point at which the DNA lesion is approximately 100% repaired, indicating that chromatin reassembly occurs concomitant with DSB repair (Figure 1D and 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1D and 1B.

claim: Chromatin reassembly occurs concomitant with DSB repair.
source: Histone occupancy returned to the pre-damage levels at the 6–8 hr time point, which is the same time point at which the DNA lesion is approximately 100% repaired, indicating that chromatin reassembly occurs concomitant with DSB repair (Figure 1D and 1B).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the temporal correlation between DNA repair and histone reassembly.

claim: The histone H3 disassembly around the DSB progressively diminished at 500bp and 750bp from the break as compared to 200bp from the I-PpoI site.
source: The histone H3 disassembly around the DSB progressively diminished at 500bp and 750bp from the break as compared to 200bp from the I-PpoI site (Figure 1D), while no conspicuous histone H3 loss was observed at either 1000bp (Figure 1D) or 3000bp (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) from the break.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: No conspicuous histone H3 loss was observed at either 1000bp or 3000bp from the break.
source: The histone H3 disassembly around the DSB progressively diminished at 500bp and 750bp from the break as compared to 200bp from the I-PpoI site (Figure 1D), while no conspicuous histone H3 loss was observed at either 1000bp (Figure 1D) or 3000bp (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) from the break.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The chromatin disassembly corresponds to a region of approximately 8 nucleosomes being disassembled during DSB repair in human cells.
source: This corresponds to a region of approximately 8 nucleosomes being disassembled during DSB repair in human cells.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the distance measurements showing histone loss up to 750bp on each side of the break.

claim: The observed histone H3 disassembly around a DSB does not appear to be a consequence of persistent DNA end resection, because the DNA level (ChIP input) around the I-PpoI-induced DNA breaks was not significantly affected by induction of DSBs.
source: Importantly the observed histone H3 disassembly around a DSB does not appear to be a consequence of persistent DNA end resection, because the DNA level (ChIP input) around the I-PpoI-induced DNA breaks was not significantly affected by induction of DSBs (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing stable DNA levels around the break.

claim: Knockdown of RAD51 had no detectable effect on the kinetics of DSB cutting and repair compared to knockdown with a scrambled RNA.
source: Knockdown of RAD51, the recombinase in HR, had no detectable effect on the kinetics of DSB cutting and repair compared to knockdown with a scrambled RNA, indicating that efficient repair of the I-PpoI site occurs in the absence of HR (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Efficient repair of the I-PpoI site occurs in the absence of HR.
source: Knockdown of RAD51, the recombinase in HR, had no detectable effect on the kinetics of DSB cutting and repair compared to knockdown with a scrambled RNA, indicating that efficient repair of the I-PpoI site occurs in the absence of HR (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the RAD51 knockdown data.

claim: Knockdown of KU80 led to the more rapid accumulation of breaks and no detectable repair.
source: By contrast, knockdown of KU80, a key factor in NHEJ, led to the more rapid accumulation of breaks and no detectable repair (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: NHEJ is the major pathway involved in the repair of this I-PpoI site in asynchronous cells.
source: This result indicates that NHEJ is the major pathway involved in the repair of this I-PpoI site in asynchronous cells, and is consistent with the failure to observe a DNA repair defect upon RAD51 knockdown.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the KU80 and RAD51 knockdown data.

claim: That repair of the I-PpoI break requires KU80 but not RAD51 is not a consequence of effects of the knockdowns on the cell cycle because flow cytometry analysis detected no apparent change in the cell cycle phase distribution.
source: That repair of the I-PpoI break requires KU80 but not RAD51 is not a consequence of effects of the knockdowns on the cell cycle because flow cytometry analysis detected no apparent change in the cell cycle phase distribution (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Efficient chromatin disassembly and reassembly occurs during RAD51 knockdown.
source: As additional evidence that chromatin disassembly and reassembly around the DSB was occurring during NHEJ, we observed efficient chromatin disassembly and reassembly during RAD51 knockdown (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Chromatin disassembly still occurs in the KU80 knockdown.
source: Furthermore, chromatin disassembly still occurs in the KU80 knockdown (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating that chromatin disassembly occurs prior to recruitment of the core NHEJ machinery.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Chromatin disassembly occurs prior to recruitment of the core NHEJ machinery.
source: Furthermore, chromatin disassembly still occurs in the KU80 knockdown (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating that chromatin disassembly occurs prior to recruitment of the core NHEJ machinery.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the KU80 knockdown data showing chromatin disassembly without KU80.

claim: Addition of either MRE11 exonuclease inhibitor PFM39 or MRE11 endonuclease inhibitor PFM03 had no effect on histone H3 disassembly and reassembly during DSB repair.
source: Addition of either inhibitor had no effect on histone H3 disassembly and reassembly during DSB repair (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: DNA end resection and HR are not required for histone H3 disassembly around DSBs in human cells.
source: Taken together these results indicate that DNA end resection and HR are not required for histone H3 disassembly around DSBs in human cells.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the MRE11 inhibitor and RAD51 knockdown data.

claim: ATM is primarily activated by blunt-ended DSBs.
source: Whereas ATM is primarily activated by blunt-ended DSBs, activation of ATR is mostly triggered by ssDNA lesions (Rhind, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Activation of ATR is mostly triggered by ssDNA lesions.
source: Whereas ATM is primarily activated by blunt-ended DSBs, activation of ATR is mostly triggered by ssDNA lesions (Rhind, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Inhibition of ATR did not disrupt the histone H3 disassembly and reassembly around the DSB.
source: Inhibition of ATR did not disrupt the histone H3 disassembly and reassembly around the DSB (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Upon ATM inhibition, DNA repair was less efficient.
source: Upon ATM inhibition, DNA repair was less efficient, as would be expected given the many roles of the DNA damage checkpoint in promoting DNA repair events (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Upon ATM inhibition, chromatin disassembly was delayed by about 2 hr as compared to the DNA cutting.
source: Upon ATM inhibition, chromatin disassembly was delayed by about 2 hr as compared to the DNA cutting, where the time point of maximal DNA cutting (3 hrs) showed no significant chromatin disassembly (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The maximal loss of histones was less pronounced around the DSB upon ATM inhibition, with histone occupancy dropping to only about 75% at the time points where DNA was 50% cut.
source: In addition, the maximal loss of histones was less pronounced around the DSB upon ATM inhibition. Specifically, histone occupancy dropped to only about 75% at the time points where DNA was 50% cut during ATM inhibition (Figure 3B), in comparison to the drop of histone occupancy to about 50% at the time points where DNA was 50% cut in the absence of inhibitor.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: ATM promotes timely and efficient nucleosome disassembly around a DSB.
source: As such, ATM promotes timely and efficient nucleosome disassembly around a DSB.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the ATM inhibition data.

claim: The results of inhibition of both ATM and ATR were not significantly different from those obtained from ATM inhibition alone.
source: The results of inhibition of both ATM and ATR were not significantly different from those obtained from ATM inhibition alone.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Budding yeast Fun30 promotes DNA end resection and chromatin disassembly around DSBs.
source: Budding yeast Fun30 promotes DNA end resection and chromatin disassembly around DSBs (Costelloe et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: SMARCAD1 promotes end resection.
source: Its mammalian counterpart SMARCAD1 promotes end resection, presumably in a similar way (Rowbotham et al., 2011) (Costelloe et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: There was a pronounced delay in the chromatin disassembly around the DSB upon SMARCAD1 knockdown.
source: Consistent with SMARCAD1 playing a role in chromatin disassembly, there was a pronounced delay in the chromatin disassembly around the DSB, upon SMARCAD1 knockdown (Figure 4A lower panel) as compared to scrambled RNA knockdown (Figure 4A, and data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The kinetics of induction of the DSB was similarly delayed upon SMARCAD1 knockdown, indicating that the delayed chromatin disassembly was a consequence of the delayed DNA cutting.
source: However, the kinetics of induction of the DSB was also similarly delayed (Figure 4A top panel), indicating that the delayed chromatin disassembly was a consequence of the delayed DNA cutting and that SMARCAD1 played no role in promoting chromatin disassembly in the inducible DSB system that we were using.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing correlated delays in DNA cutting and chromatin disassembly.

claim: SMARCAD1 played no role in promoting chromatin disassembly in the inducible DSB system.
source: However, the kinetics of induction of the DSB was also similarly delayed (Figure 4A top panel), indicating that the delayed chromatin disassembly was a consequence of the delayed DNA cutting and that SMARCAD1 played no role in promoting chromatin disassembly in the inducible DSB system that we were using.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: The induction of the I-PpoI endonuclease itself was markedly reduced upon SMARCAD1 knockdown.
source: However, we found that the induction of the I-PpoI endonuclease itself was markedly reduced upon SMARCAD1 knockdown (Figure 4B), which was presumably due to a role of SMARCAD1 directly or indirectly in its expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The reduced I-PpoI induction upon SMARCAD1 knockdown was presumably due to a role of SMARCAD1 directly or indirectly in its expression.
source: However, we found that the induction of the I-PpoI endonuclease itself was markedly reduced upon SMARCAD1 knockdown (Figure 4B), which was presumably due to a role of SMARCAD1 directly or indirectly in its expression.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about the mechanism underlying the observed effect.

claim: INO80 was previously shown to bind DSBs and assist DSB repair in yeast.
source: The remodeling complex INO80 (Inositol requiring 80) was previously shown to bind DSBs and assist DSB repair in yeast (Morrison and Shen, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: INO80 is phosphorylated by ATM in response to DSBs in yeast.
source: In addition, INO80 is phosphorylated by ATM in response to DSBs in yeast (Morrison et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Upon INO80 knockdown, the DNA breaks accumulated faster than normal.
source: Upon INO80 knockdown, the DNA breaks accumulated faster than normal (Figure 4C), which is characteristic of conditions in which DSB repair is blocked, such as the KU80 knockdown (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: DNA repair did not occur upon INO80 knockdown.
source: Indeed, DNA repair did not occur upon INO80 knockdown (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Chromatin disassembly was markedly delayed upon INO80 knockdown compared to DNA cutting.
source: Compared to DNA cutting, chromatin disassembly was markedly delayed upon INO80 knockdown.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The ATP-dependent chromatin remodeler INO80 is required for timely chromatin disassembly around a DSB in human cells.
source: These results indicate that the ATP-dependent chromatin remodeler INO80 is required for timely chromatin disassembly around a DSB in human cells.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the INO80 knockdown data.

claim: Combined inhibition of ATM in cells with INO80 knockdown led to the same degree of defect in chromatin disassembly as single INO80 knockdown.
source: Consistent with this prediction, we found that combined inhibition of ATM in cells with IN080 knockdown, led to the same degree of defect in chromatin disassembly as single INO80 knockdown (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: ASF1A knockdown led to a complete block in chromatin reassembly after DSB repair.
source: ASF1A knockdown led to a complete block in chromatin reassembly after DSB repair (Figure 5A, compare lower panel to top panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Knockdown of ASF1B led to a subtle delay in chromatin reassembly compared to the kinetics of DSB repair.
source: Meanwhile, knockdown of ASF1B led to a subtle delay in chromatin reassembly compared to the kinetics of DSB repair (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Knockdown of CAF-1 led to a major defect in chromatin reassembly after DSB repair.
source: Knockdown of CAF-1 led to a major defect in chromatin reassembly after DSB repair (Figure 5C), suggesting that the CAF-1-dependent chromatin assembly pathway is utilized during DSB repair in human cells, even in the absence of significant DNA resection or DNA synthesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The CAF-1-dependent chromatin assembly pathway is utilized during DSB repair in human cells, even in the absence of significant DNA resection or DNA synthesis.
source: Knockdown of CAF-1 led to a major defect in chromatin reassembly after DSB repair (Figure 5C), suggesting that the CAF-1-dependent chromatin assembly pathway is utilized during DSB repair in human cells, even in the absence of significant DNA resection or DNA synthesis.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the CAF-1 knockdown data.

claim: Knockdown of HIRA led to a complete block in chromatin reassembly after DSB repair with two independent shRNAs.
source: We observed that knockdown of HIRA led to a complete block in chromatin reassembly after DSB repair with two independent shRNAs (Figure 5D), demonstrating that replication-independent chromatin assembly is also important for restoring the chromatin structure after DSB repair in human cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Replication-independent chromatin assembly is important for restoring the chromatin structure after DSB repair in human cells.
source: We observed that knockdown of HIRA led to a complete block in chromatin reassembly after DSB repair with two independent shRNAs (Figure 5D), demonstrating that replication-independent chromatin assembly is also important for restoring the chromatin structure after DSB repair in human cells.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the HIRA knockdown data.

claim: The replication-dependent and replication-independent chromatin assembly pathways are interdependent for restoring the chromatin structure following DSB repair.
source: Because there is very little chromatin assembly after DSB repair in the absence of CAF-1 and virtually no chromatin assembly after DSB repair in the absence of HIRA, it would appear that the replication-dependent and replication-independent chromatin assembly pathways are interdependent for restoring the chromatin structure following DSB repair (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined CAF-1 and HIRA knockdown data.

claim: Nucleosome disassembly and reassembly around DSBs is a highly regulated and coordinated part of the cellular response to DSB damage in mammalian cells, even during repair pathways that do not involve DNA resection.
source: Here we have shown that nucleosome disassembly and reassembly around DSBs is a highly regulated and coordinated part of the cellular response to DSB damage in mammalian cells, even during repair pathways that do not involve DNA resection.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from all the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Repair of DSBs by NHEJ was accompanied by the apparent complete disassembly of nucleosomes adjacent to the break, spanning up to 1500 bp around the break.
source: Repair of DSBs by NHEJ was accompanied by the apparent complete disassembly of nucleosomes adjacent to the break, spanning up to 1500 bp around the break.
evidence: This claim is based on the experimental data showing histone loss up to 750bp on each side of the break.

claim: Chromatin disassembly around the DSB is a checkpoint-stimulated response to breaks involving an ATP-dependent chromatin remodeler.
source: We found that chromatin disassembly around the DSB is a checkpoint-stimulated response to breaks involving an ATP-dependent chromatin remodeler.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the ATM and INO80 data.

claim: HIRA-mediated assembly of H3.3 and CAF-1 mediated assembly of H3.1 occur after DSB repair in an interdependent manner.
source: Meanwhile, HIRA-mediated assembly of H3.3 and CAF-1 mediated assembly of H3.1 occur after DSB repair in an interdependent manner, suggesting that coordinated mechanisms exist to accurately reestablish the epigenetic information carried by the chromatin structure after DNA repair (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the HIRA and CAF-1 knockdown data.

claim: Coordinated mechanisms exist to accurately reestablish the epigenetic information carried by the chromatin structure after DNA repair.
source: Meanwhile, HIRA-mediated assembly of H3.3 and CAF-1 mediated assembly of H3.1 occur after DSB repair in an interdependent manner, suggesting that coordinated mechanisms exist to accurately reestablish the epigenetic information carried by the chromatin structure after DNA repair (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is based on speculation from the experimental data.

claim: Previous work showed that histone H3 loss occurs around a DSB in asynchronous human cells.
source: In agreement with our findings, previous work has shown that histone H3 loss occurs around a DSB in asynchronous human cells (Goldstein et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In a previous study, histone H3 loss was not detected during G1 phase when NHEJ is the predominant form of repair for the non-nucleolar regions of the genome.
source: However, in that study histone H3 loss was not detected during G1 phase when NHEJ is the predominant form of repair for the non-nucleolar regions of the genome (Goldstein et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In a previous study, the observed H3 loss around a DSB within the rDNA locus in asynchronous cells reached over 7 kb away from the break ends with no clear decrease at this distance from the break.
source: Notably, their H3-H4 loss reached over 7 kb away from the break ends with no clear decrease at this distance from the break, suggesting it could be a lot more extensive (Goldstein et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In the current study, histone H3 was disassembled during NHEJ and the histone H3 disassembly was a local event, restricted to within 0.75 kb away from DSBs.
source: By contrast, in our analyses, histone H3 was disassembled during NHEJ and the histone H3 disassembly was a local event, restricted to within 0.75 kb away from DSBs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the current study.

claim: The rDNA in humans is present in approximately 300 copies of tandem repeats and has a specialized chromatin structure, generally being heterochromatic.
source: In humans, the rDNA is present in approximately 300 copies of tandem repeats and has a specialized chromatin structure, generally being heterochromatic.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about rDNA structure.

claim: The rDNA has a unique nucleolar DNA damage response, enabling HR-mediated repair of I-PpoI-induced DSBs within the rDNA at any phase of the cell cycle, including G1, presumably templated by rDNA repeats in cis.
source: Furthermore, the rDNA has a unique nucleolar DNA damage response, enabling HR-mediated repair of I-PpoI-induced DSBs within the rDNA at any phase of the cell cycle, including G1, presumably templated by rDNA repeats in cis (van Sluis and McStay, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The chromatin disassembly study from the Kastan group was likely examining chromatin disassembly at the rDNA during homologous recombination.
source: As such, the chromatin disassembly study from the Kastan group was likely examining chromatin disassembly at the rDNA during homologous recombination (Goldstein et al., 2013), while we examined chromatin disassembly from euchromatin during NHEJ, which could explain the difference in size of the domain of chromatin disassembly.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from comparing the current study with prior work.

claim: The local histone disassembly may facilitate efficient recruitment of the NHEJ repair machinery to DSBs, while avoiding the loss of epigenetic information that would occur due to extensive histone disassembly.
source: One possibility is that the local histone disassembly may facilitate efficient recruitment of the NHEJ repair machinery to DSBs, while avoiding the loss of epigenetic information that would occur due to extensive histone disassembly.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about the function of localized chromatin disassembly.

claim: INO80 has been shown previously to be recruited to DSBs in mammalian cells.
source: INO80 has been shown previously to be recruited to DSBs in mammalian cells (Kashiwaba et al., 2010), although its exact function there was not clear.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

source: It was interesting to find a role for INO80 in promoting chromatin disassembly around a DSB, because in yeast, the role of INO80 in chromatin disassembly around a DSB is dependent on INO80's role in promoting DNA resection (Tsukuda et al., 2005; van Attikum et al., 2004).

claim: In mammalian cells, INO80 promotes chromatin disassembly in the absence of apparent DNA resection, suggesting that it can directly modify chromatin structure during DSB repair.
source: However, in our studies in mammalian cells, INO80 promotes chromatin disassembly in the absence of apparent DNA resection, suggesting that it can directly modify chromatin structure during DSB repair.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing INO80's role without DNA resection.

claim: INO80 is required to promote accessibility of the NER machinery to UV lesions in mammalian cells.
source: In agreement, INO80 is required to promote accessibility of the NER machinery to UV lesions in mammalian cells (Jiang et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The function of INO80 in chromatin disassembly at a DSB presumably depends on its histone eviction activity and its ATPase activity.
source: The function of INO80 in chromatin disassembly at a DSB presumably depends on its histone eviction activity and its ATPase activity, although further study is needed to characterize the detailed molecular mechanism.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about the mechanism of INO80 function.

claim: Chromatin reassembly occurs after DSB repair and is not required for DSB repair per se.
source: Chromatin reassembly occurs after DSB repair and is not required for DSB repair per se (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing chromatin reassembly after DNA repair is complete.

claim: ASF1A and ASF1B play non-redundant roles in histone H3 reassembly during DSB repair, with ASF1A playing an essential role while ASF1B is dispensable.
source: We found that the histone chaperones ASF1A and ASF1B play non-redundant roles in histone H3 reassembly during DSB repair, with ASF1A playing an essential role in regulating histone reassembly around a DSB, while ASF1B is dispensable for this function (Figure 5).

claim: Both HIRA and CAF-1 are recruited to sites of NER.
source: In agreement, both HIRA and CAF-1 are recruited to sites of NER, and HIRA deposits H3.3 in response to UV irradiation (Adam et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: HIRA deposits H3.3 in response to UV irradiation.
source: In agreement, both HIRA and CAF-1 are recruited to sites of NER, and HIRA deposits H3.3 in response to UV irradiation (Adam et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: HIRA has been shown to mediate a gap-filling mechanism of H3.3 deposition without the need for transcription or any sequence specificity, given the non-specific DNA binding ability of HIRA.
source: Indeed, HIRA has been shown to mediate a gap-filling mechanism of H3.3 deposition without the need for transcription or any sequence specificity, given the non-specific DNA binding ability of HIRA (Ray-Gallet et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The defect in chromatin reassembly upon CAF-1 knockdown is unlikely to be due to indirect effects on cell cycle progression, because the defect was localized specifically to the region around the DSB.
source: It is unlikely that these results are due to indirect effects of CAF-1 knockdown, for example on cell cycle progression, because the defect in chromatin reassembly was localized specifically to the region around the DSB.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the spatial specificity of the observed effect.

claim: All the cells would not have had a chance to progress through S phase within the short time course of cutting and repair that occurred in the experiments.

source: The role of CAF-1 in chromatin assembly after DSB repair is not due to an indirect effect on HIRA levels, because no change in HIRA protein level was seen upon knockdown of CAF-1.

evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: A concerted mechanism between replication-dependent and replication-independent chromatin assembly pathways may be necessary to allow faithful reassembly of chromatin structures after DSB repair, perhaps in order to enable the accurate re-establishment of transcription programs.
source: Such a concerted mechanism may be necessary to allow faithful reassembly of chromatin structures after DSB repair, perhaps in order to enable the accurate re-establishment of transcription programs.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about the function of coordinated chromatin assembly.

claim: Immediately following the induction of DSBs in mammalian cells, histone disassembly occurs on both sides of the break, with only about 4 nucleosomes disrupted on each side of the DNA break.
source: In conclusion, we propose that immediately following the induction of DSBs in mammalian cells, histone disassembly occurs on both sides of the break. This step is tightly regulated as only about 4 nucleosomes are disrupted on each side of the DNA break, presumably for efficient recruitment of the NHEJ repair machinery.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing localized histone loss.

claim: ATM and histone remodelers such as INO80 actively participate in the histone disassembly during DSB repair.
source: ATM and histone remodelers such as INO80 actively participate in the histone disassembly.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the ATM inhibition and INO80 knockdown data.

claim: After DSB repair, histones are reassembled back to the repaired DNA regions to restore their local chromatin structures, and this step requires functional coordination between histone chaperones ASF1A, CAF-1 and HIRA.
source: After DSB repair, histones are reassembled back to the repaired DNA regions to restore their local chromatin structures, and this step requires functional coordination between histone chaperones ASF1A, CAF-1 and HIRA.
